question: How does LoRA compare to full fine-tuning?

checked_by.who: AI agent (Claude Opus 5), driven by the repository owner
checked_by.not: This is not a human expert review. No domain expert read these papers for this record.
checked_by.method: Layer 1 resolved every reference against its primary registration record: arXiv abstract pages for arXiv preprints, Crossref for publisher-deposited DOIs, DataCite for arXiv DOIs. OpenAlex was consulted only to corroborate; where records differed, the primary publisher record was taken as authoritative. Layer 2 read the full text where a legally public copy existed (arXiv PDF, PubMed Central), and fell back to the abstract otherwise. Each claim records which tier its evidence came from.
limits: Existence and relevance were judged separately: a paper can be real and still not bear on the question.
A claim the sources do not mention is recorded as unverified. That is not a finding that the claim is false.

One source (R2) is paywalled in its published form; the evidence quoted for it comes from the arXiv preprint, which carries a different title. That version difference is recorded on every claim that rests on it.

Most verdicts rest on abstracts even where the full text was retrieved: where a claim was fully addressed by the abstract, that is what the verdict cites. Only 3 of 17 quotes come from inside a paper body.

claims.claim: LoRA significantly reduces computational and memory costs compared to full fine-tuning by optimizing only low-rank adaptation matrices instead of all model parameters

evidence.quote: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ... mitigates this challenge by optimizing only low-rank adaptation matrices, thereby greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters.
Its small memory footprint allows practitioners to adapt large models to specific tasks at a fraction of the cost of full finetuning.
evidence.note: The quoted passage is the paper's abstract. The full text was retrieved and searched as well, but this verdict rests on the abstract.

evidence.quote: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduce this cost by introducing low-rank matrices for tuning fewer parameters.
Low-rank adaption (LoRA) is a widely used parameter-efficient finetuning method for LLM that reduces memory requirements.

limits: The sources assert reduced cost; none of the four quantifies the reduction in the passages cited here.

searched.result: The word 'generalization' occurs once, on p.19, about initialization schemes in a theorem appendix. Nothing about LoRA's generalization versus full fine-tuning.
Mentions that on-device models 'poorly generalize to downstream tasks due to their limited sizes' -- about model size, not about LoRA versus full fine-tuning.

established: LoRA reduces the compute and memory cost of adaptation relative to full fine-tuning, by training low-rank matrices instead of all parameters. Four of the ten sources state this directly.
Full fine-tuning is described as prohibitive or infeasible for large models by four of the ten sources, in both general-NLP and on-device settings.

LoRA improves communication efficiency in federated and edge settings. Both supporting sources evaluate a proposed variant rather than plain LoRA, and neither states the mechanism the synthesis gives for it.
Where to place LoRA adapters is unsettled in the literature. This rests on a single source reporting the state of the field, not on two retrieved papers disagreeing.
established_with_limits: Parameter-efficient methods can approach full fine-tuning on average, and LoRA gave about a 4.5-fold training speed-up in one study. That study is on protein language models (ESM2 3B), not general LLMs, and the parity result comes from a paper whose own analysis says these methods are "no match for FT in performance under most cases" before averaging.
not_established: That performance trade-offs across model sizes and task types are insufficiently characterised.
That the relation between LoRA rank and task complexity needs further investigation.
That long-term effects of LoRA on generalization versus full fine-tuning are poorly understood.
public_summary.not_established_note: These three appear in the generated synthesis but could not be traced to anything in the retrieved papers. That is a failure to find support, not a finding that they are wrong.
public_summary.retrieval: All ten cited papers exist and every title matches its registration record. Three of the ten do not bear on the question, and one of those is a general-relativity paper about electric charge and gravity.
